blocks.text: Sequence-to-sequence loss applies the same cross-entropy foundation covered earlier in this module to tasks that transform an entire input sequence into a different output sequence, translation, summarization, and rewriting among the most common examples, computing loss specifically over the generated target output.

This topic clarifies how sequence-to-sequence loss relates to the causal language modeling loss covered in the previous topic, since modern decoder only models handle sequence-to-sequence tasks using largely the same underlying mechanism.
1. What Sequence-to-Sequence Tasks Need From a Loss

blocks.alt: What Sequence-to-Sequence Tasks Need From a Loss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959286-950431117.png

A sequence-to-sequence task takes an entire input sequence and produces an entire output sequence in response, translating a sentence, summarizing a document, and the loss function needs to measure how well the generated output sequence matches the correct target sequence, token by token.
2. Encoder-Decoder vs Decoder-Only Framing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959286-269957599.png

Historically, sequence-to-sequence tasks were often handled by dedicated encoder-decoder architectures, but modern decoder only models, covered in the Foundation Models module, handle these same tasks by simply treating the input as a prompt and generating the output as a continuation, using the same causal language modeling loss covered in the previous topic.
3. Computing Loss Only Over the Target Sequence

blocks.alt: Computing Loss Only Over the Target Sequence
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959286-702093485.png

Just as supervised fine-tuning masks loss away from the prompt tokens, covered in the Causal Language Modeling Loss topic, sequence-to-sequence loss is computed only over the target output sequence, not the input sequence the model is conditioning on, ensuring training signal focuses entirely on the generation the model actually needs to learn.

code.content:
# A simplified sequence-to-sequence loss with input masking
predictions = model(input_sequence_tokens + target_sequence_tokens)
loss_mask = [0] * len(input_sequence_tokens) + [1] * len(target_sequence_tokens)
loss = masked_cross_entropy(predictions, targets, loss_mask)

blocks.text: 4. Handling Variable Length Outputs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959286-522522026.png

Sequence-to-sequence tasks naturally produce outputs of varying length, a short summary versus a long one, and computing loss as a per token average, the same convention covered in the previous topic, keeps the loss value meaningfully comparable across examples regardless of how long each specific target sequence happens to be.
5. Teacher Forcing During Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100278-357872373.png

During training, the model is typically shown the true target tokens generated so far, rather than its own possibly imperfect predictions, when predicting the next target token, a technique called teacher forcing that keeps training stable and efficient, distinct from how the model generates at inference time, one predicted token at a time with no access to a ground truth answer.

blocks.title: Training and inference differ in an important way here
blocks.content: This gap between teacher forcing during training and genuine autoregressive generation at inference time is a known, well studied consideration for sequence-to-sequence tasks, sometimes contributing to a model performing somewhat differently once deployed than its training loss alone would suggest.

blocks.text: 6. Sequence-to-Sequence Loss vs Causal Language Modeling Loss

blocks.alt: Sequence-to-Sequence Loss vs Causal Language Modeling Loss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100280-998591855.png

For a decoder only model, sequence-to-sequence loss is not a fundamentally different mechanism from the causal language modeling loss covered in the previous topic, it is the same underlying calculation, simply applied to a task where the input naturally divides into a source portion and a target portion to generate.

blocks.text: 7. Padding and Masking in Sequence-to-Sequence Loss

Since input and target sequences both vary in length across a batch, padding, covered in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, and the resulting attention and loss masks need to correctly account for both the input and target portions of every example, a slightly more involved masking setup than a purely single sequence causal language modeling case.
8. Common Sequence-to-Sequence Tasks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100280-942097823.png

Translation, summarization, and various forms of rewriting or reformatting text are among the most common sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning tasks, each fitting the same input sequence to target sequence shape, with the loss computed identically over the target portion regardless of which specific task it is.
9. Evaluating Beyond the Loss Value

While loss gives a useful training time signal, sequence-to-sequence task quality is typically evaluated further using task specific metrics, covered in depth in this course dedicated Evaluation module, since a lower loss does not automatically guarantee the generated output is genuinely fluent or faithful to the source in the way a human reader would judge.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a model to summarize long articles structures each training example with the article as the input portion and the correct summary as the target portion, masking loss so it only applies to the summary tokens, exactly following the sequence-to-sequence loss pattern covered in this topic.

Their loss curve decreases steadily during training, and combined with a separate task specific evaluation, covered in the Evaluation module, they confirm the resulting model produces genuinely useful, faithful summaries, not just summaries that happened to minimize the training loss value.
Common Mistakes

items: Computing loss over the input source sequence as well as the target, diluting the training signal
Assuming sequence-to-sequence loss requires a fundamentally different mechanism from causal language modeling loss for a decoder only model
Relying on loss value alone to judge sequence-to-sequence output quality without task specific evaluation
Not accounting for both input and target sequence lengths when setting up padding and masking

blocks.text: Practice

For a translation example with a source sentence and its target translation, sketch which tokens should be masked out of the loss calculation and which should have loss computed, confirming you understand where the source to target boundary belongs.
Key Takeaway

Sequence-to-sequence loss applies the same causal language modeling loss mechanism specifically to the target output portion of a task that transforms an input sequence into a different output sequence, and for modern decoder only models, this is not a separate loss function so much as the same underlying calculation applied with masking that focuses training signal on the generated target.
